cells.why: Step 1: in OBJ a persisted commit is one conditional PUT to the object store (Q put). Step 2: a real store's PUT p99 is about 80 ms on S3 Standard and at or above 7.3 ms on Express One Zone (cited in E-28). Step 3: P-01's bar is C + 5 ms = 5.7 ms on this box. So every persisted write misses the bar on a real store; MinIO on this disk (p99 2.7 ms) has no network and no replication.
cells.why2: Step 1: a `persisted` write commits by one conditional PUT to the object store (R `obj`, Q `put`). Step 2: that PUT costs p99 2.67 ms on local MinIO, but about 30 ms typical on S3 Standard and at or above 7.3 ms p99 on Express One Zone (cited in E-28). Step 3: the bar is C + 5 ms = 5.7 ms here, so on any real store the write p99 is over it; E-28's own threshold puts OBJ out at `persisted`.

cells.why: Judge 2 was right; I confirm the steps. (1) In v4 any member takes a write and cells merge by last-writer-wins on Lamport stamps (SPACE section 2: R `lww`; O `lamp`, 'no total order per partition'). (2) So two members that each take a write to another field of one row apply the two in opposite orders: one copy shows {x} then {x, y}, the other {y} then {x, y}, and no one log has both as folds of its prefixes. (3) P-01 asks for per-partition order, which REQUIREMENTS reads as total, and tests that every replica equals the fold of the committed log; v4 has no such log, and getting one needs another row's R and O options. Judge 1's verdict here was the default text about E-22's Raft prototype, which is not v4's mechanism.

cells.why: With writer time as the median (A-23) no row expired early and every copy removed a row at the same log position (E-21: 30 seeds in each of nine families; E-22: 100 seeds in 3 modes). Not shown: the pin that an expiry tick over 1e6 rows costs only what expires. The bound is read as writer time while a writer exists; read to the letter, a failover near the ttl made expiry 2,036 ms late against 350 ms in E-22, in any one-writer design (the alt).
cells.closes: The expiry-tick pin at 1e3 to 1e6 rows once L2's TTL index is built (phase 2); the user's word on the bound's wording (E-22 D9).
cells.why2: Writer time as the median (window 0, A-23) passed every TTL check where at most one clock is wrong: worst 100 ms early and 300 ms late against 250 and 350 ms, and copies agreed at each position (E-21, simulated, 30 seeds a family). E-22's cache check passes with a leader change; a row is then up to 2.0 s late, which E-21 and this verdict read as time with no writer. Not shown on any kernel: the O(expired) tick pin at 1e6 rows, and memtier against Redis (PERF-02).

cells.why: E-31 model-checked the subscribe protocol in state and log modes on ten bounds (up to 7.6 million states): with A-06's END answer and per-slot cursors, a snapshot then deltas has no gap and no overlap across a leader crash, a reload, a slot move and a relay. E-22's check (a one-hop miss, shortfall, the 1 KB bound, a follow that ends equal) passed in 100 seeds in 3 modes. For the rows without slots, nothing moves in LANE, and E-17's models carry a reader across a split (lineage) and a re-key (the old cursor is refused and the reader restarts from a snapshot).

E-22's near-cache check (a one-hop miss, `shortfall`, the memory bound) passes 100 of 100 seeds in three modes. A client cursor is 22 to 79 B (E-19).

cells.why: E-22's check passed in 100 seeds in 3 modes (300 of 300 partitions linearizable): six readers that miss one key at once make one load, and a write that lands during the load wins, because the fill is a conditional write judged at the writer. The test's 1,000 misses were run as six.
cells.why2: On the prototype six readers on three servers and three clients, missing one key at once, made exactly one `load` (it runs at the key's writer and fills with `if: absent`), and a write during the load kept its value. Both held in 100 of 100 seeds in three modes, with a leader change and a slot move inside (E-22, simulated). The number of readers does not enter the mechanism, so 1,000 misses give the same one load (reasoned).

cells.why: E-22's check passed in 100 seeds in 3 modes (300 of 300 partitions linearizable): six readers that miss one key at once make one load, and a write that lands during the load wins, because the fill is a conditional write judged at the writer. The test's 1,000 misses were run as six.

The number of readers does not enter the mechanism, so 1,000 misses give the same one load (reasoned).

Step 1: CELL's positions are group offsets (O off), and it grows by a re-key into a new generation of groups. Step 2: as written, a cursor of the old generation is refused and the reader restarts from a snapshot (E-17, model-checked); a raw group offset breaks at the first move in 5 steps (E-31). Step 3: so a log reader that holds a kept position does not get the records after it once and in order across a re-key. The form that keeps positions (rekey-carry) puts a sequence in each record, which is another O option.
cells.why2: Step 1: CELL's positions are group offsets (O `off`), and it grows by a re-key that copies rows into a new generation of groups. Step 2: as written, a cursor of the old generation is refused `unknown-log` and the reader restarts from a snapshot (E-17c's model; SPACE §2 `rekey`: 'cursors break'); kept without the refusal, offsets give a false `expired` in 5 steps (E-31, `off`). Step 3: so a log reader cannot go on from a kept position after the resource grows: it skips records or reads them again, against 'a position never changes meaning across scaling' and 'every record once, in order'.

cells.why: Judge 2 was right; I confirm the steps. (1) P-13 has two halves: a lapsed session's rows go on every copy within its lease plus one tick, and a live session's rows never go; whether a session has lapsed is a condition on its renewals, by one clock. (2) v4 has no time rule (T is empty in SPACE 4.1) and no one writer to judge a condition (R `lww`; DESIGN-V5 section 9 measured two claims judged on local state that both committed). (3) So a member that has not seen a renewal removes a live session's rows, and the remove stands if its stamp is higher; or renewals win, and a late one brings a removed row back (STATUS's open bug: a write from an evicted member beats a newer remove). One half breaks either way, and the cure is another row's R and T options. Judge 1 named the same gap and called it open.

cells.why: Step 1: the rule must be judged by one writer per partition. Step 2: under R lww any replica accepts a conditional write on its own state, so two sells of the last item through two servers both pass. Step 3: v4 measured exactly that: both ok (REQUIREMENTS P-14, DESIGN-V5 9).
cells.why2: Step 1: a rule over a partition holds only if every condition is judged at one writer. Step 3: so two sells of the last item through two servers both pass.

cells.why: Step 1: BUY's only condition is JetStream's 'expected last sequence of this subject', and a row is one subject. Step 2: so a rule over a partition of several rows cannot be judged as one; the only wider check is the whole stream's last sequence, which any other write breaks (E-44 gap 4, reasoned from the headers). Step 3: the judge is the client, not the one writer: it reads, computes and retries (about 4 ms an op, 34 % of publishes wasted at 8 writers). For one row at a time it holds: one ok in 100 of 100 rounds.
cells.why2: Step 1: on JetStream a condition is a check-and-write by the client against one subject's last sequence. Step 2: that judges one row; a partition of several rows can only be checked against the whole stream's last sequence, which any other write breaks (E-44, gap 4, reasoned from the headers). Step 3: so a rule over a partition of several rows cannot be kept, though two sells of one row gave exactly one `ok` in 100 of 100 rounds.

Real Elle finds G0 in 0 of 300 histories with the lock rule, against 10 to 19 of 100 without it (E-22b). The saga is an L5 library on fenced locks, the same in every saga row.

cells.why: E-22's rebuild check passed in 100 seeds in 3 modes, and `history: 'all'` kept every record. But byte for byte fails today for some views: a `sum` view depends on the order of records (0.10000000000000003 where a rebuild gives 0.1, E-43) and top-k breaks ties by arrival (E-23). A-10's contract fixes both in E-23's harness (0 mismatches in 225.6 million checks), but it is not landed in data. Every row runs the same data.
cells.closes: data's contract change and the view rule (A-10; a SCHEDULE_VERSION bump), then the rebuild test on random runs.
cells.why2: On the prototype the rebuilt projection equalled the live one in every seed, and `history: 'all'` kept every record (E-22). But E-43 found a `sum` view that depends on the records, not the rows (0.10000000000000003 live against 0.1 rebuilt), and two data commits under one SCHEDULE_VERSION that fold 578 rows differently. The fix is owed by data for every row alike (A-10: an exactly rounded sum, the fold-version pins) and has not landed.

cells.why: V4's dedup is a window (D win) and it takes no A-05 mark. E-30's model shows that a window option applies a derived output twice after a restart past its horizon (12 to 13 steps), and E-44 saw a window fail past its horizon on a real system.
cells.why2: Step 1: 'each A record affects B exactly once' needs A's log in one order, and outputs deduped at B's one writer. Step 2: v4 has neither a position in A (O `lamp`) nor a writer-side judge (R `lww`); REQUIREMENTS F-02 records that one forwarded write can commit twice. Step 3: so an output that is not idempotent (an `incr`) can apply twice after a crash mid-batch.

cells.why: E-40 measured a prototype client over wss: data plus the client is 27.9 KB gzip against 60 KB, a cold Chromium page reaches its first committed write in 17 ms and a Web Worker in 13 ms with one TLS handshake plus two round trips by design, and the import costs 4 to 22 ms against 50 ms. The client is TypeScript in every row and WebSocket carries the same frames (A-11); the cursor promises are E-31's, and E-45 built the RESP gateway. Bun, Deno and a real edge runtime were not run.
cells.why2: A prototype client (the door, follow with a cursor, writes that resolve on commit) with all of data is 27.9 KB gzip against 60 KB. It reaches its first committed write over wss in 13 to 17 ms in Chromium, with one TLS handshake plus two round trips by design, and imports in 4 to 22 ms against 50 ms (E-40). A RESP gateway built from the API's verbs ran with 0 errors (E-45); P-03's promises over this wire are E-31's model.

cells.why: Judge 1 was right. cells.why: Step 1: 'takeable by the writer's clock' needs one clock per partition that every take is judged by. Step 2: V4 has no writer and no time rule (R lww, T none): each replica judges a take on its own state and its own clock. Step 3: so a replica whose clock runs ahead hands a delayed message out early, and two replicas can hand out the same one (as in P-09).
cells.why2: Step 1: 'takeable within one tick of its time by the writer's clock' and a take with a lease need writer time and `claim` at one writer. Step 2: v4 has neither (T is empty; R `lww` has no conditions, SPACE §5). Step 3: so two members can hand out one delayed message, each by its own clock.
